articles.title: Meet Cathal Sweeney, the 16-year-old Irish student who turned the frustration of losing hurling balls in winter darkness into a glow-in-the-dark ball that generated €40,000 in four months
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For Cathal Sweeney, a frustrating problem on the hurling pitch became the starting point for an innovative student business. A self-described hurling .
articles.body: For Cathal Sweeney, a frustrating problem on the hurling pitch became the starting point for an innovative student business. A self-described hurling enthusiast, Sweeney found that training on dark winter evenings could be difficult when there was not enough light to see the sliotar clearly. Rather than accepting the problem, he developed a glow-in-the-dark ball designed to help players continue practising when daylight fades. The idea eventually became GLO Hurling and its flagship product, the Glo Ball. In 2026, GLO Hurling won the Senior Category at the Student Enterprise Programme National Finals. Sweeney, a student at Mungret Community College in Limerick, developed the product as part of his Student Enterprise project. According to the official Student Enterprise Programme, the idea arose from his frustration when trying to train during dark winter evenings.A solution for darker eveningsThe Glo Ball was designed to address a practical challenge faced by hurling and camogie players who want to continue training when natural light is limited. The ball uses phosphorescent material, which absorbs light and gradually emits it over time, creating a glow effect. The technology allows the sliotar to remain visible in darker conditions. To create a longer-lasting glow, Sweeney paired the ball with a high-strength UV light. This combination is intended to improve the ball's visibility and make it suitable for training when daylight is unavailable. According to the official Student Enterprise Programme profile, the Glo Ball was designed for both children and adults who play hurling or camogie, offering a potential solution for players training during darker periods of the year.From an idea to a businessWhat began as a response to a personal frustration developed into GLO Hurling, Sweeney's student enterprise. According to RTÉ, Ireland's national public service broadcaster, the Glo Ball generated €40,000 in sales within four months of its launch. The project went on to achieve national recognition at the 2026 Student Enterprise Programme National Finals, where GLO Hurling won the Senior Category. The official winners' list identifies the business, representing Mungret Community College in Limerick, as the top entry in its category. The achievement placed Sweeney's idea among a range of student-led businesses developed through the national programme, which encourages secondary school students to create and develop their own enterprise ideas.An everyday problemThe story behind the Glo Ball highlights how simple, everyday problems can sometimes inspire practical innovations. For Sweeney, the challenge was finding a way to continue hurling practice when winter darkness made training more difficult. His response was to rethink one of the sport's most familiar pieces of equipment and develop a sliotar that could remain visible after daylight faded. The result was a product built around a specific need: helping hurling and camogie players continue practising in low-light conditions.The idea also shows how innovation does not always begin with a complicated scientific breakthrough. Sometimes, it starts with a problem that many people encounter and a willingness to look for a different solution.A winning ideaBy turning that challenge into a working product and student business, Sweeney's GLO Hurling earned national recognition in Ireland's 2026 Student Enterprise Programme. The Glo Ball combines a traditional piece of sporting equipment with phosphorescent technology and UV charging to create a practical training tool for darker conditions. For Sweeney, the idea began with the simple frustration of trying to train on a dark winter evening. It eventually developed into an award-winning student enterprise and a reminder that useful ideas can emerge from the everyday problems people encounter in the activities they enjoy most.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Missouri grandma started serving free breakfasts to neighbors in a town of fewer than 300; months later, health officials said she needed a permit to continue
articles.summary: US News: In a small Missouri town, where mornings can sometimes feel more quiet than the rest of the world, one grandmother made her kitchen an unlikely meetin.
articles.body: In a small Missouri town, where mornings can sometimes feel more quiet than the rest of the world, one grandmother made her kitchen an unlikely meeting place. It began as a simple act of cooking breakfast for a few familiar faces, but has evolved into a beloved local tradition, bringing neighbors together over coffee, homemade food and conversation. But a letter from county health officials several months into the tradition cast doubt on the future of those breakfasts. Kathy Kite, a Harrisburg, Mo., grandmother, has been serving neighbors free breakfasts since May, Fox News Digital reported. The town has fewer than 300 people and what started as a meal for a few people quickly morphed into a regular community event.Kite's concept was born from an experience at the local gas station where she works. The station stopped serving breakfast after the COVID-19 pandemic, she said, but regulars kept asking about breakfast. Kite didn’t want the tradition to die out, so she invited some of them over to her house and started making breakfast herself. Her answer was bigger than she had expected. More residents started to stop in for coffee and breakfast, Fox News Digital reported. Meetings turned into occasions when neighbors would tell stories, talk about farming and the weather and reminisce about their childhoods. Later, local mothers also brought their children before school.For Kite, breakfasts were about so much more than food. She said that the people who visit her house are an extension of her family and that she didn’t want to stop providing for them.Letter from county health officials changes thingsIn July, though, Kite received a letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department and the situation changed. But the department told her she needed to get a food permit to keep serving food to the public, Fox News Digital reported. Kite said the letter frightened and upset her because she read it to mean she could be fined or jailed if she continued the breakfasts without complying. Later she posted the letter on Facebook and her story was noticed and supported by people in the community. But the county health department denied threatening Kite with jail time.Why a permit may be requiredThe crux of the dispute seems to be how Missouri’s food regulations define the breakfasts of Kite. The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department, which spoke to Fox News Digital, said food prepared for family and friends does not require a permit. But officials said a permit is needed when food is provided to the public under Missouri food code. The department also said when the complaint concerning Kite was received her home had several features that are typical in a food establishment. These are said to have included an open sign, a tip jar, food promoted on social media and a sign in the yard. According to officials, the department got involved after receiving a complaint that someone got sick from food served at the establishment. The department said its mission is to promote safe food-handling practices and prevent foodborne illness.Kite says the requirements would be crushingKite told Fox News Digital that to comply with the requirements described to her, she would need to install a commercial kitchen in her home. She said that could potentially run into hundreds of thousands of dollars and argued that such an investment would be unreasonable for someone who provides free meals. Kite lives in a house that’s about 115 years old and said she doesn’t want to alter the historic property for a commercial kitchen. She has also invited local officials to her home to see for themselves how she prepares the food. Her argument is simple. She is a grandmother cooking for friends, neighbors and members of her community, not a conventional restaurant.Legal questions in the disputeThe controversy has also attracted the attention of the Goldwater Institute, which sent a letter to the Boone County health department demanding answers about the legal basis for the requirements, Fox News Digital reported. The director of allied litigation for the group, Dave Roland, blasted what he called excessive government regulation of an act of neighborly kindness. No lawsuit had been filed at that point, though legal action was still possible, the institute said. The dispute, then, poses a bigger question of where the line should be drawn between informal community food-sharing and running a food establishment.Health officials say there are optionsThere are ways for people to share homemade food with their communities with and without a food permit, said health officials, although the county and Kite differ on the circumstances. The department also said Kite had not been cited or issued a cease-and-desist order, and it again said it did not threaten her with jail time. Officials said their goal is to partner with people and businesses to ensure food is prepared and served safely. To Kite, though, it’s a deeply personal issue.Her breakfasts began as an effort to fill a void, the closing of the gas station’s morning food service. They became an excuse for the residents of a small town to gather, to talk and to share a meal. The resolution of the permitting dispute still holds the key to how breakfasts continue in their current form. But the story has already highlighted the unusual importance a simple homemade breakfast can take on in a small community — becoming, for many residents, less about the food, and more about having a place where neighbors feel like family.Images Courtesy: Fox NewsCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Elizabeth Quigley: I'm leaving the BBC after MS pain made it hard to carry on
articles.summary: Elizabeth Quigley, wife of first minister John Swinney, is leaving the BBC on health grounds after almost 27 years.
articles.body:
I have lived and worked with multiple sclerosis for 26 years, almost as long as I have been a BBC Scotland journalist, but recently I have been absent from the airwaves.

I've been struggling with a condition called trigeminal neuralgia that causes excruciating pain like an electric shock across the side of my face, which can stop me from speaking, eating or drinking.

It's not part of everyone's life with MS but it has recently become part of mine - and being unable to speak is not great for a broadcaster.

Thanks to my neurologist and the NHS team looking after me, I've managed to regain my speech and reduce the amount of discomfort I'm in - but the pain can, and does, reappear.

So, unfortunately, I've had to make the very difficult decision to leave the BBC on health grounds.

Before I started here in November 1999, I had previously worked for the Scotsman, Scotland on Sunday and the Scottish Daily Mail.

I was just 28 when I became the BBC's first female political correspondent in the new Scottish Parliament. Three months later I was diagnosed with MS.

I had been having a strange feeling of pins and needles in my face and was convinced it was a problem with my wisdom teeth. It wasn't.

A swift MRI scan confirmed it was multiple sclerosis.

I was shocked. I had vaguely heard about MS but I really knew nothing about the degenerative disease.

I wasn't offered any kind of treatment. All I was advised to do was to keep healthy and avoid stress.

That was easier said than done for a journalist who often worked in live television and radio news.

But, at first, I had no symptoms and I could continue in my job without anyone knowing for several years.

By 2007, I couldn't keep covering up my stumbling with excuses and so felt I had to reveal my diagnosis.

By that stage I had moved away from political reporting and had met and married the MSP John Swinney , who would later become a Scottish government minister and is now the first minister of Scotland.

The year after I revealed my MS diagnosis I turned it into journalism, making television and radio documentaries about the condition .

I told how Scotland was believed to have the highest rates of multiple sclerosis in the world and concluded by saying that finding a cure - or even some answers as to why it's so common here - would definitely be a very good ending to my story.

Almost two decades later that has not yet happened.

In 2010, our son Matthew was born and I discovered even more about MS.

During pregnancy, my symptoms largely disappeared, my walking improved as did my dexterity in typing and writing.

I learned that this can happen to some women with MS.

But when I looked into it more, I discovered it also happens to some woman who have other autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and thyroid problems.

The relief from my symptoms continued for another nine months after Matthew was born but then returned.

When I investigated this strange phenomenon - and made a radio documentary on the subject - I discovered that hormones have a major part to play and that more research definitely needs to be done.

My marriage to John Swinney meant I stepped away from political reporting but I have covered many other stories including a groundbreaking film about a woman whose sense of smell could help diagnose Parkinson's.

Many changes have happened since I was diagnosed in 2000.

There were very few disease-modifying therapies back then - now there are about 20.

I was initially diagnosed with relapsing remitting MS. Now, I have secondary progressive.

The tingling in my face has largely disappeared, but my walking has become increasingly difficult over the years.

I need crutches or a rollator - what I call my wheels - and sometimes I need a wheelchair.

Far from trying to disguise my disability and cover it up, I chose to quite openly stand using a crutch on the steps of Bute House when my husband became first minister.

I've always maintained that you can live life well with MS - it might just have to be a bit differently. And my career proves that.

Recording interviews and editing at home, for example, have been some of the ways to make this work but adapting and reinventing have always been part of my journalistic career.

I've worked with many fabulous, talented and caring individuals over my time at the BBC.

I am very grateful to everyone who has helped me continue in the job I have loved for so many years.

But now the time has come to close this chapter and start a new one.

articles.title: Nepal floods: How two reports warned of this disaster months ago
articles.summary: South Asia News: Months before the devastating floods struck Nepal and Tibet, two landmark reports by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICI.
articles.body: Months before the devastating floods struck Nepal and Tibet, two landmark reports by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) had warned that rapidly melting glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya(HKH) were escalating the risks of catastrophic floods and other cryosphere-related disasters.Released in March 2026, the reports found that glacier ice loss across the region had doubled since 2000, with the smallest and most vulnerable glaciers shrinking rapidly and intensifying hazards such as glacial lake outburst floods.It also revealed that glaciers have lost up to 27 metres of ice thickness since 1975The warnings have come into sharp focus after a catastrophic flash flood triggered by a glacier collapse struck the Nepal-China border region this week, killing hundreds and leaving nearly 1,000 people missing.Researchers are investigating whether an ice-rock avalanche from a high-altitude location triggered the disaster.ICIMOD cryosphere specialist Mohd Farooq Azam told news agency PTI that the incident involved the detachment of bedrock from beneath a glacier, with ice and rock cascading down into the valley.“This is basically an ice and rock avalanche. So, as per current understanding, there is a detachment of the bedrock, which means that the bedrock from below the glacier is detached from its position and came down to the valley that created this disaster,” Azam said.HKH glaciers lost 12% of their area in three decadesThe two ICIMOD reports, Changing Dynamics of Glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya Region from 1990 to 2020 and HKH Glacier Outlook 2026: Insights from 50 Years of Himalayan Glacier Monitoring, provide a detailed assessment of glacier change across the region.According to the reports, HKH glaciers lost around 12% of their total area and 9% of their estimated ice reserves between 1990 and 2020.The Hindu Kush Himalaya contains the largest volume of ice outside the polar regions, with more than 63,700 glaciers covering nearly 55,782 square kilometres.Also read: Himalayan glaciers shrinking at alarming pace, ice loss doubled in 21st century, says ICIMODThese glaciers feed at least ten major Asian river systems and support food, water, energy and livelihoods for billions of people downstream.ICIMOD said around 78% of the glacier area, located between 4,500 and 6,000 metres above sea level, is highly exposed to elevation-dependent warming.“This isn’t a distant problem; it’s a crisis unfolding in real-time, with new disasters every summer and monsoon,” Pema Gyamtsho, director General of ICIMOD, said.“The fact that ice loss rates have doubled this century should shock us all into action,” he added.Smaller glaciers face faster losses and rising hazardsThe ICIMOD analysis found that the region's smallest glaciers are shrinking more rapidly than others.“Between 1990 and 2020, HKH glaciers lost about 12% of their total area, but the losses are most acute for the region’s smallest glaciers—those below 0.5 km²—which are shrinking more rapidly than others,” Sudan Bikash Maharjan, remote sensing analyst at ICIMOD and lead author of the glacier dynamics report, said.He warned that the trend poses immediate risks of localised water shortages for high mountain communities and intensifies hazards such as glacial lake outburst floods.Three-fourths of the region's glaciers fall within this vulnerable size category, according to ICIMOD.Flood-hit valley faces risk of secondary flash floodThe immediate situation in Nepal has also highlighted another danger associated with debris and temporary lakes formed after major mountain disasters.Azam told PTI that debris from the ice-rock avalanche has accumulated at a river confluence, creating a temporary dam. Water is continuing to collect behind it, raising concerns about a possible secondary flash flood.“This dam is collecting water, and it is expected that over the next three days, there will be more water collected in this temporary pond or lake,” he said. “So, there are chances that there may be some secondary flash flood in this valley.”He added that the lake could also breach gradually without causing a flash flood.The lake formed after the landslide began overflowing on Friday, prompting panic in areas already devastated by the floods.Its reservoir had held more than 2.5 million cubic metres of water, up from an estimated 1.5 million to 2 million cubic metres a day earlier, before overflowing into the Bhotekoshi River.Also read: Second flood 'imminent'? Nepal halts rescue ops as China border lake begins overflowingNepal temporarily halted rescue operations, while Chinese rescue personnel and vehicles were moved to safer locations due to concerns over the dammed lake.‘Critical decade’ for Himalayan cryosphereThe HKH Glacier Outlook 2026 synthesised data from 38 monitored glaciers and found that widespread glacier wastage had doubled after 2000.However, ICIMOD also highlighted significant gaps in monitoring. Of the 38 glaciers, only seven meet the global benchmark monitoring standards set by the World Glacier Monitoring Service.Major glacierised regions, including the Karakoram, Sikkim, Zanskar and Bhutan, remain largely unmonitored.“We are trying to navigate a rapidly changing future with an incomplete map,” Azam said in the ICIMOD report.“Without expanding our monitoring networks and standardising methodologies, accelerated changes in water flows and cryosphere risks could remain undetected until the impacts are severe.”The reports identified the eastern Hengduan Shan mountains as the area with the highest percentage of glacier loss, with some areas losing up to 33% of their glacier area in three decades.The largest absolute losses, however, were concentrated in the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra basins, which contain more than 74% of the region's glaciers.Why regional cooperation mattersThe Nepal-Tibet disaster has also underlined the cross-border nature of mountain hazards.Azam said that floods and glacial disasters occurring upstream do not recognise national boundaries.“In this particular case, we see that the disaster happened in the Nepal Himalaya and downstream, it immediately entered into the Tibetan boundary, where it hit the infrastructure there and then again it came down towards Nepal,” he said.“This is why we need to have a regional cooperation and data sharing policy to better understand these disasters and perhaps to be ready for such disasters in advance,” Azam added.The ICIMOD reports have called for a major expansion of glacier monitoring, better standardisation of methodologies and greater investment in climate-resilient adaptation planning.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1992, Congress ordered the removal of 2 dams blocking the Elwha River—24 years later, the river finally ran free to the Sea
articles.summary: US News: In 1992, Congress passed an Act of law that few outside Washington State took much notice of at the time, yet it would go on to reshape one of the Pac.
articles.body: In 1992, Congress passed an Act of law that few outside Washington State took much notice of at the time, yet it would go on to reshape one of the Pacific Northwest's great rivers. According to the Elwha River Ecosystem and Fisheries Restoration Act, the federal government was to buy up two hydroelectric dams that had blocked salmon from reaching their spawning grounds for the best part of a century, and to tear them down once and for all. They had to balance the ecological case for removal against the needs of a local paper mill, a city water supply, and the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, all of whom depended on the river in different ways. It took until 2011 for demolition crews to finally arrive on site. Three years later, in 2014, the job was done, and for the first time in a hundred years the Elwha ran free from the mountains to the sea.$29.5 million plan for Elwha River dam removalThe Act did not simply order the dams torn down overnight. Instead, it set out a careful legal and financial process for the federal government to acquire the two facilities before any demolition could begin. According to Section 3 of the Act, the Secretary of the Interior was authorised "to acquire the Elwha and Glines Canyon Projects, and all rights of the owner and local industrial consumer therein, subject to the appropriation of funds therefor," but only once it had been established that dam removal was genuinely necessary for full ecological restoration.Crucially, the law fixed the price of that acquisition. As per the Act, "the consideration for acquisition of the Projects shall be $29.5 million and no more," to be paid to the dams' owner and to the local industrial consumer, the Port Angeles pulp and paper mill that depended on the power the dams produced. The Act also required the Secretary to prepare a detailed report by January 1994 examining the costs, alternatives and feasibility of removal, including, according to the Act, "the timetable after conveyance for removal of the dams and the plans for removal and disposal of sediment, debris, and other materials."Congress protected local water supplies during Elwha River dam removalLawmakers were careful to ensure that restoring the river would not come at the expense of the communities that had grown to rely on it. Reportedly, Section 4 of the Act required the Elwha River dam removal plan to protect local water supplies, "protection of the existing quality and availability of water from the Elwha River for municipal and industrial uses from possible adverse impacts of dam removal," with the cost of any necessary water treatment works to be borne by the federal government rather than residents.The Act also dealt with the question of power supply. Since the mill on Ediz Hook depended on electricity generated by the dams, Section 5 directed the Bonneville Power Administration to deliver so-called "project replacement power" once the dams were gone, ensuring the mill's operations would not simply collapse once the turbines stopped turning. Provision was likewise made for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, with Section 7 authorising up to $4,000,000 for the purchase of land held in trust for the tribe's, as per the Act, "housing, economic development, and moorage for the Tribal commercial fishing fleet."Elwha River dam removal took decades before work began in 2011Turning an Act of Congress into a working demolition project took decades rather than years. Funding, environmental review and engineering preparation for removing dams of this size, the largest dam removal project in American history at the time, meant that construction crews did not begin dismantling the Glines Canyon and Elwha Dams until 2011. According to the Act, annual licences for the dams were to remain in force "until the date the Secretary has acquired title to the Projects," a condition that took many years to satisfy.The patience embedded in the 1992 law eventually paid off. By 2014, both dams had been fully removed, and the Elwha River began carrying sediment and nutrients down to the Strait of Juan de Fuca for the first time in a century. Salmon returned to stretches of river they had not reached since before the dams were built, fulfilling the ambition set out, as per the Act, at the very start: the full restoration of "the Elwha River ecosystem and native anadromous fisheries." Twenty-four years after Congress put pen to paper, the Elwha once again flowed unbroken from the peaks of the Olympic Mountains to the sea.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal and China briefly halt rescue efforts as barrier lake overflows
articles.summary: More than 580 people dead and more than 2,400 missing after the flash flood disaster that struck on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Nepal and China have resumed rescue efforts for survivors of the devastating flash flood that hit the border region two days ago, following a brief suspension as a “barrier lake” formed during the disaster began to overflow.

Chinese rescue teams and vehicles were forced to pull back to safe ground, state broadcaster CCTV reported, as the risk of the lake bursting rose. Nepalese authorities also paused search operations for 90 minutes, an army officer confirmed on Friday.

“As the risk posed by the upstream dammed lake was deemed manageable, rescue operations for the Gyirong mudslide disaster quickly resumed and were stepped up,” CCTV said.

Nepal’s army spokesperson said the rise in water level comprised just 0.6 metres (two feet).

Rescuers earlier feared the “barrier lake”, formed as Wednesday’s flash flood carried huge volumes of mud and debris down a steep valley, could unleash another huge and destructive wave.

In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, residents were seen scrambling up hillsides to escape potential surges in the river level, according to the Reuters news agency.

The disaster unfolded as a glacier collapsed and sent a huge torrent of ice, water, rock, and mud down Himalayan river valleys, burying entire villages and destroying roads, bridges, and hydropower plants.

In its wake, leftover debris trapped water to form a barrier lake, a natural dam created when landslides block a river.

With water continuing to pour into the lake, the threat to downstream communities of another wave of flooding rose. China deployed an engineering team to conduct aerial surveys and 3D modelling of the site.

By Friday afternoon, however, the secondary flood scare was confirmed to be “nowhere near” the magnitude of Wednesday’s disaster, said David Fisher, the delegation head for the Nepal International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

The lake overflow added to “ongoing terror” rocking communities who have lost their homes, finding refuge in schools and government buildings, Fisher told Al Jazeera.

“It’s an extremely difficult time,” he added.

The death toll from the disaster continues to rise. On Friday, Nepal’s disaster authority reported at least 579 deaths, with 1,924 people missing.

Chinese authorities reported on Friday that the death toll in Tibet has now risen to at least five, with 558 people missing.

Bishal Nath Upreti, president of the Nepal Centre for Disaster Management, told Al Jazeera that conditions are “extremely difficult” for those trapped in the disaster zone, as destroyed roads have left them completely cut off.

Nepal’s disaster authority said a total of 4,451 people had been rescued as of Friday, with 16 helicopters carrying out 99 rescue flights so far.

Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing, said the number of missing is expected to rise. China has deployed about 500 military and paramilitary personnel and sent Premier Li Qiang to supervise operations on the ground, while Nepal has deployed 30,000 security personnel to search remote, cut-off valleys, she said.

More ⁠than ⁠90,000 people are estimated to have been affected ⁠by disaster, the ⁠IRFC’s Fisher said on Friday.

Teams have been unable to reach some of the hardest-hit areas in Rasuwa, which remains accessible only via helicopter.

“We’re very concerned for them,” Fisher said.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flash floods: These two women are among nearly 300 Indians missing
articles.summary: Her family is among hundreds anxiously waiting for news after the deadly flash floods.
articles.body:
Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.

She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.

Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.

Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.

The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years.

Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.

But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message.

"After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.

Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.

The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement.

In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square.

She told her husband the countryside was beautiful.

"She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."

The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.

She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night.

She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.

Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one.

A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.

There was little to suggest what was coming.

"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."

The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.

Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.

After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.

Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck.

"I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."

At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.

He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.

The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since.

"Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."

He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards.

"Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."

Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."

For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.

They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.

Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.

Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."

Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family.

"She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."

She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said.

The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre.

Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.

"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."

For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.

Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains.

Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.

Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list of 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.

For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

articles.title: Too much assistance? Why Nepal declined help but agreed for aid from India, China & others
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal has declined offers from several countries, including India and China, to send specialised search-and-rescue teams, as it battles one of its wor.
articles.body: Nepal has declined offers from several countries, including India and China, to send specialised search-and-rescue teams, as it battles one of its worst flood disasters in years. It said that its own security agencies are capable of handling the operation.The decision comes even as 517 foreign nationals remain missing following the Bhotekoshi floods, with nationals of India, China, the US, Malaysia, Ukraine, the UK, Australia, Canada and several other countries among those unaccounted for.However, Nepal's foreign Shishir Khanal clarified that Nepal had not turned down assistance from friendly nations or the international community. He said the government was ready to seek international technical expertise if rescue efforts involved specialised challenges, particularly tunnels or other complex structures.“Where we need additional technical capacity, we will cooperate as necessary,” The Himalayan Times quotes Khanal as saying, adding that Nepal remained in touch with friendly countries and would seek technical support depending on the specific requirements of the rescue operation.At first glance, Nepal's decision appears counterintuitive. With hundreds missing and rescue operations underway in difficult terrain, additional manpower and specialised equipment from neighbouring countries could potentially help. Yet Kathmandu appears to be drawing a distinction between accepting humanitarian assistance and allowing foreign rescue teams to operate on its soil.Lesson from 2015 earthquakeThe key reason behind Nepal's decision lies in its experience during the devastating 2015 earthquake.According to a senior foreign ministry official, Nepal's government remembered the coordination and management problems that emerged when large numbers of foreign search-and-rescue teams arrived after the earthquake. The presence of multiple teams, along with competition among countries, created difficulties in managing the response.This time, the Balen Shah-government has therefore opted for a more centralised approach. The decision was reportedly taken on the recommendation of the Nepali Army and police, which believe Nepal's own security agencies can manage the search-and-rescue operation.The foreign ministry official summed up the decision: “We received similar requests from China and other countries too, but we had to turn down the request,” the Kathmandu Post quoting foreign ministry official saying.Why say no to teams, but yes to aid?Nepal's approach does not amount to shutting the door on international assistance altogether.Instead, Kathmandu has asked foreign governments to channel financial contributions through a one-door mechanism, the Prime Minister's Relief Fund. Officials have indicated that additional financial aid and other support will be sought during the reconstruction phase.That distinction is significant. Foreign rescue teams mean multiple governments and agencies operating simultaneously on the ground, potentially creating overlapping chains of command, logistical demands and coordination problems. Financial assistance, by contrast, allows Nepal's authorities to retain control over how resources are distributed and where they are needed.An emergency response team (ERT) has been set up which would "serve as the central coordinating body within the ministry to facilitate search, rescue, information verification, and consular assistance in respect of foreign nationals affected by, missing in, or otherwise connected to the flood incident,” a foreign ministry statement said according to The Post.India, China and others offered helpIndia was among the countries seeking to send a rescue team. After hundreds of Indian nationals went missing or lost contact, New Delhi requested permission to deploy the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) to Nepal. China and several other countries also made similar requests.The ministry of external affairs said on Friday that it was waiting for a response from the Nepal government."We have also made a specific offer to the Nepal authorities to dispatch NDRF teams along with their associated equipment that can help in ongoing search and rescue operations and bring relief assistance to people impacted by the tragedy. We await a response from the government of Nepal on this front. We stand ready to offer any assistance that the Nepal authorities might require," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said.India has already sent more than 47.5 tonnes of relief supplies to Nepal, including medicines and food packets. It has also offered Bailey bridges and prefab truss bridges to support relief and connectivity.The US, UK and World Bank have also announced financial support, while the Asian Development Bank has offered longer-term assistance aimed at improving Nepal's disaster preparedness, early-warning systems and infrastructure resilience.US secretary of state Marco Rubio said Washington was ready to provide humanitarian assistance, while British foreign secretary Ed Miliband expressed support and sought updates on rescue efforts involving missing British nationals.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII?
articles.summary: Haakon becomes the king at a turbulent time for Norway's monarchy.
articles.body:
King Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill.

King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death.

Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden.

Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway".

Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps.

As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent.

King Haakon VIII takes the throne in Norway following death of Harald V

"I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells.

Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected.

"King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother.

"But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill."

Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.

His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne.

Haakon was ahead of his older sister, Princess Märtha Louise, in the line of succession.

The constitution was changed in 1990 to give women the right to inherit the throne, so Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra is in line to be Norway's first female head of state since the 15th Century.

Haakon has become the king at a turbulent time for Norway's royal family.

The monarchy remains broadly popular among Norwegians and has been long praised for its modern outlook.

But in recent years it has been beset by scandal.

Only this year, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, now Queen of Norway, has apologised for several years of ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son has been convicted of rape in a high-profile trial. Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from an earlier relationship, is appealing against the conviction.

Born in 1973, King Haakon is the youngest child of the late king and Queen Sonja.

By Haakon's own admission, he struggled at times to accept his royal status in his early years.

"Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it... ​At school it made me anxious," he wrote in his 2023 autobiography, recalling his days in a state primary school in the 1980s.

He became crown prince in 1991 at the tender age of 17, following the death of his grandfather King Olav V.

Unusually for a royal, he was educated at local state schools before embarking upon a four-year-long naval career, graduating from the Norwegian Naval Academy in 1995.

He decided not to follow his father and grandfather to Oxford University, instead flying to California to enrol at the University of Berkeley, where he studied political science.

Soon after his return to Norway, Haakon met his now-wife Mette-Marit at a music festival in her home city of Kristiansand in 1999.

She was dubbed by the press as the Cinderella of Kristiansand - a reference to her humble beginnings.

"What we two found together was so strong that I could not let it go," the then-Crown Prince Haakon said of Mette-Marit ahead of their wedding in 2001.

But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating.

Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936.

Queen Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier.

She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession.

The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either.

What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king.

In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s.

She did not say whether she had taken them herself.

It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention.

The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus.

In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy.

Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy.

Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone."

But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism.

Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo.

Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal.

Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

Several polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen.

Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis.

Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.

Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own".

"But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says.

"What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime."

Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task".

"I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V."

Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy.

articles.title: Want to know what's really in your food? The Trump administration is trying to help
articles.summary: Trump's HHS proposed a rule requiring food manufacturers to notify the FDA about GRAS food additives, closing a loophole exposed by tara flour illnesses.
articles.body: Americans have a right to know what is in their food. That shouldn’t be controversial. You should be able to walk into a grocery store, read a label, and be confident that the ingredients listed on the food you are buying have been subject to transparent, science-based oversight and are safe for consumption. The Trump administration has now taken an important step toward doing exactly that. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) proposed a rule requiring food manufacturers to notify the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) whenever they determine that an added substance is Generally Recognized as Safe, or "GRAS." When Congress passed the Food Additives Amendment in 1958, the idea was simple: ingredients with a documented history of safe use or those that qualified experts had agreed were safe should not face the same pre-market approval process as brand-new food additives. Everyday substances like salt, vinegar, black pepper, and baking powder fall into this category. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION EXPANDS 'PRODUCT OF USA' LABEL AS PUSH FOR AMERICAN-RAISED BEEF GROWS Unfortunately, our regulatory system has fallen short of that basic standard. And over time, the exception became the rule. Under the current system, manufacturers can self-determine whether a new additive is GRAS and introduce it to the U.S. food supply without notifying the FDA or the public. The manufacturer is still responsible for maintaining evidence to support its own determination, but the FDA may have no advance notice when a new substance enters the supply chain. And that is the problem. The FDA cannot effectively oversee substances and ensure our health if it does not know they are entering the food supply, and Americans cannot make fully informed choices when our system lacks transparency. That’s a loophole. GEN Z TURNS ON CLASSIC SNACKS, FORCING MAJOR GROCERY SHAKE-UP: 'THEY DON'T TRUST THEM' One that has allowed large food manufacturers to flood the domestic food market with new substances without FDA review or even FDA notification. We’ve raised this issue before at the America First Policy Institute (AFPI). Last year, we laid out this problem in an issue brief, "Make America Healthy Again by Ensuring Safe Foods," calling for greater transparency and accountability in the GRAS process. RFK JR HAILS FIRST US HOSPITAL TO PROMISE HEALTHIER MEALS: 'WE HAVE A TEMPLATE' The proposed rule would require the FDA to maintain a public list of GRAS notices, giving researchers, regulators, and consumers visibility into ingredients entering the marketplace. For substances already on the market, the Trump administration is proposing a streamlined process to ensure the public has transparency about what is in their food. This is exactly how you modernize our food system and close loopholes: increase transparency and give responsible manufacturers a path to compliance. We’ve already seen why reform is necessary. Consider tara flour, a food additive that entered the food supply without the manufacturer submitting a GRAS notice to the FDA. After hundreds of illnesses and hospitalizations were later associated with the substance, the FDA conducted its own review and found that tara flour did not meet the standard for GRAS. We should learn from that experience. But this shouldn’t be confused with the choice between consumer safety and a thriving food industry. Manufacturers that promote transparency in the products they sell benefit from consumer confidence. Companies that invest in safety and transparency should not be put at a disadvantage by a system that lets competitors introduce substances into the food supply without regulatory oversight. Americans should not have to wait for people to get sick before regulators identify the substances and ingredients entering our food system. This is not about government dictating every decision made at the dinner table, but about ensuring consumers have access to transparent, reliable information on what they’re eating. BROOKE ROLLINS, DR. BEN CARSON: WE ARE PUTTING REAL FOOD BACK ON SCHOOL LUNCH TRAYS President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are getting that right, taking a step toward restoring accountability in a flawed system that has drifted far from its original purpose. Regulators gain insight into what is reaching the food supply, manufacturers don’t circumvent transparent rules, and families have all the facts they need to make their own choices. If a substance is safe enough to put on Americans’ plates, requiring manufacturers to tell the FDA should not be controversial. articles.title: Uber Eats drone delivery could soon reach your home
articles.summary: Uber Eats drone delivery launches later this year through a Zipline partnership, starting in Dallas and Houston with a goal of one million daily flights.
articles.body: Your next Uber Eats order could arrive without a car pulling up outside your home. Uber Eats drone delivery is moving closer to everyday life through a new partnership with Zipline, one of the most established names in autonomous delivery. Uber and Zipline announced the deal earlier this month. The companies say the first deliveries will begin later this year in existing Zipline markets. From there, they plan to expand into dozens of U.S. cities. Their long-term target is huge: 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029. That does not mean a drone will show up with your meal tomorrow. The rollout will start in markets where Zipline already operates, including Dallas and Houston, before expanding to additional areas. Zipline already has commercial delivery systems operating in the U.S., which gives this partnership a running start. Here's how the system works and what you could expect if drone delivery reaches your neighborhood. THIS SATURDAY! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. PAPA JOHNS DRONE DELIVERY SKIPS THE PIZZA How Uber Eats drone delivery with Zipline will work The experience should eventually feel much like placing any other Uber Eats order. The companies say eligible Uber Eats customers will have the option to receive their orders through Zipline when the service launches later this year. Today, customers in Zipline's existing U.S. service areas can download the Zipline app, enter their address and browse available restaurants and stores. Once someone places an order, the business prepares it and loads it into Zipline's autonomous delivery system. Zipline handles the flight with its Platform 2 system, also called P2. The electric aircraft can carry up to 8 pounds and has a 10-mile service radius. Zipline says the system can make some 10-mile deliveries in about 10 minutes. Its current fact sheet lists a cruise speed of about 70 mph. When the aircraft reaches the delivery location, it hovers around 300 feet above the ground. A smaller delivery unit descends on a tether, steers toward the selected drop-off spot and gently places the order on the ground. The delivery unit then returns to the aircraft, and the drone flies back to recharge for its next order. Zipline told CyberGuy that the entire process happens autonomously. So you do not need a drone landing pad next to the house. Zipline can place deliveries in a yard or another approved location while the larger aircraft remains overhead. Zipline already delivers to real homes According to the joint announcement, Zipline has completed more than 2.7 million commercial deliveries. Its aircraft have flown more than 135 million autonomous commercial miles. Zipline also says it now makes a delivery somewhere in the world every 20 seconds. In the U.S., its P2 home delivery system has already been operating with Walmart and restaurant partners. Zipline's fact sheet says the service launched in Pea Ridge, Arkansas and more than 20 communities around Dallas-Fort Worth. The company has been expanding quickly as well. In July, Zipline said the number of businesses offering delivery through its app had grown 13 times during the first half of 2026. Roughly 70% of its flights were taking place in the United States at that point. CyberGuy recently looked at another side of that expansion when Zipline began carrying eligible prescriptions to Cleveland Clinic patients. The drone stays overhead while a tethered unit lowers the medication to the patient's property. Your dinner could spend less time in traffic The obvious appeal is speed. A drone can take a more direct path than a car crawling through traffic. It also avoids the hunt for parking near a busy restaurant. Zipline says its P2 system can make some 10-mile trips in about 10 minutes. Of course, that does not mean every meal reaches your house 10 minutes after you tap Place order. The restaurant still needs to prepare the food. Severe weather or certain flight conditions could still affect whether a drone can complete a delivery. Local flight conditions may also change what the system can do. Still, cutting time on the road could help your dinner spend less time getting cold in the back seat of a car. MISSOURI TESTS MEDICAL DRONES TO SPEED UP RURAL HEALTH CARE Uber wants several ways to deliver your order The Zipline deal also reveals a bigger part of Uber's strategy. Uber says it is building a delivery network that combines human couriers with autonomous technology. Depending on the trip, that technology could include a sidewalk robot or a drone. We have already seen pieces of this plan. Uber Eats uses autonomous sidewalk robots in some markets. CyberGuy previously looked at how those machines navigate streets and bring food directly to customers. Uber also invested in drone company Flytrex in 2025. At the time, Uber called that its first investment in drone delivery technology. Now Zipline joins the picture. That suggests Uber wants the Uber Eats app to become the layer connecting customers with different delivery systems. A drone may make sense for one neighborhood. A robot may work better somewhere else. You may eventually care less about what carries your dinner and more about which option gets it there faster. What about all that drone noise? Noise could be one of the first things people notice when drone delivery arrives in their neighborhood. One delivery overhead may be easy to ignore. Regular flights throughout the day could be another story. Zipline says it has spent years working to make its aircraft quieter. The company says its drones now typically fly at least 300 feet above the ground. During delivery, the aircraft stays high while a smaller unit lowers the order on a tether. Zipline says the full delivery takes about 90 seconds. Flying higher helps reduce how much sound reaches people below. Still, the real question is how noticeable these drones will be once they become part of everyday neighborhood traffic. Safety could determine how fast drones spread A delivery service flying over homes has a much higher bar than the hobby drone someone sends up at the park. Zipline's aircraft fly autonomously with onboard systems that help them understand their surroundings. The company has also received FAA approval for certain beyond visual line of sight, or BVLOS, operations. That allows approved flights without requiring ground observers to watch the aircraft along the entire route. Zipline says it put P2 through extensive testing before launching home deliveries. That included tens of millions of simulated flights and more than 150,000 deliveries at test facilities. However, regulatory approval does not automatically mean drone delivery can appear everywhere. The companies still need the right operating area and infrastructure before a neighborhood can participate. Uber is putting money behind the idea Uber is also making a strategic investment in Zipline as part of the agreement. The companies have not disclosed the size of that investment in their official announcement. However, they describe the relationship as a long-term effort to accelerate drone delivery across the U.S. Zipline itself has plenty of money riding on this expansion. Earlier this year, the company announced that it had raised more than $600 million and reached a valuation of $7.6 billion. The companies now have a very ambitious benchmark in front of them. Reaching one million drone deliveries every day by the end of 2029 would require far more aircraft and participating businesses. The network would also need to reach many more homes. CyberGuy reached out to both Uber and Zipline for comment, but neither company responded before our deadline. What this means to you Most Uber Eats orders will continue arriving the familiar way for now. However, if you live in an area where Zipline already operates, watch the Uber Eats app later this year. The companies say qualifying customers will eventually have the option to receive an order by drone. Before selecting drone delivery, pay attention to the drop-off location. You should also check what happens when weather prevents a flight. Then look closely at the price. Uber and Zipline have yet to explain whether customers will pay an additional fee for the drone option. If the cost stays reasonable, speed could become the selling point. Waiting for dinner feels a lot longer when your phone says a drone could get it there in minutes. The larger change may happen almost without us noticing. Once people stop thinking of drone delivery as unusual, choosing one could eventually feel as routine as selecting a faster delivery window today. Kurt's key takeaways I've watched drone delivery go from something that felt years away to something people are actually starting to use. What jumps out to me here is how quickly Uber could help push it into the mainstream. Millions of people already know how to order dinner through Uber Eats, while Zipline already has drones making real deliveries. Put those two pieces together and this starts to feel a lot closer to everyday life. Of course, people will have questions once these drones start showing up over their neighborhoods. How much noise will they make? Will the delivery really be faster? And how much extra will Uber charge for the convenience? For me, that last part could be the dealbreaker. If a drone can get my food to me noticeably faster without adding a hefty fee or becoming a neighborhood nuisance, I can see a lot of people giving it a try. The real test will come when that drone delivery option actually pops up on your phone, and you have to decide whether you want dinner coming by road or through the sky. Would you choose a drone if it could get your Uber Eats order to your door faster, or would you rather keep delivery traffic on the ground? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: With Kuwait deal, Pakistan expands defence umbrella across Middle East
articles.summary: From Kuwait to Saudi Arabia, Gulf states are deepening defence ties with Pakistan, but its own gains remain unclear.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan and Kuwait signed a new defence agreement on Thursday, with Pakistan’s Ministry of Defence saying it significantly enhances a military cooperation framework in place since 2023.

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and his Kuwaiti counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah Ali Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah, signed the “Protocol Agreement-2026” in Rawalpindi.

Under the deal, Pakistan’s armed forces will help train Kuwait’s military, build its defence capacity and assist with border management, the ministry said in a statement.

The deal builds on an underlying agreement signed in June 2023 but only formally ratified by Kuwait last month.

The agreement is the latest in a growing list.

In recent years, Pakistan has signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia, joined a trilateral collective-security agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye called the “Mecca Pact”, deployed thousands of troops and a fighter squadron to Saudi Arabia, and deepened training arrangements with Qatar.

Pakistan has offered training and manpower to Gulf militaries for decades. What has changed is the pace and visibility of that role, and the readiness of Gulf capitals to formalise it through signed agreements rather than quiet cooperation.

The question raised by this run of agreements is less about any one pact than the pattern itself: Why do Gulf states keep turning to Pakistan, and what does Pakistan gain by saying yes?

Kuwait is the most recent Gulf state to turn to Islamabad.

Defence cooperation with Kuwait dates to the late 1960s. In the 1990-91 Gulf War, Pakistan sent a large military contingent to Saudi Arabia, positioned defensively around Mecca and Madinah after Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990.

Zahid Mahmood, a former two-star Pakistani general and now a defence analyst, said that history is the backdrop to Thursday’s signing. “Pakistan-Kuwait defence collaboration is not new,” he told Al Jazeera.

According to Mahmood, the deal cannot be compared with the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) that Pakistan signed with Saudi Arabia last September. It contains no clause resembling the central commitment of the Mecca Pact or the SMDA, both of which treat aggression against one signatory as aggression against all.

The partnership with Kuwait includes training, logistics, intelligence sharing and joint exercises, overseen by an annual joint military committee.

“What we can say is that Kuwait appears to be moving from basic defence cooperation towards a more structured security partnership. It doesn’t mean there’s an Article 5-style collective-defence commitment in place. But it is considerably more institutionalised and structured than before,” Mahmood said.

Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, told Al Jazeera the new agreement gives Pakistan a role not just in developing Kuwait’s broader defence capabilities but specifically in securing its border with Iraq.

“If Pakistani troops get deployed to Kuwait and are positioned on its border, it essentially brings this agreement closer to the Pak-Saudi one,” he said. “For now, Pakistan’s defence engagement with Gulf states is beginning to take a more concrete shape. While it still is not essentially a security umbrella, it is helping these states diversify their defence partnerships and add another layer of deterrence.”

Yousef Al-Mulla, a retired Kuwaiti air force major-general, made a similar point to the pan-Arab outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, noting that Pakistan’s growing military-industrial capability and nuclear status give it “strategic weight”.

Analysts believe confidence in Washington’s Gulf security guarantees weakened after Israel struck a compound hosting Hamas officials in Doha, Qatar, in September 2025. The Hamas leaders were part of a team of negotiators involved at the time in indirect negotiations with Israel, when Israel bombed Qatar.

Days later, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the SMDA.

During the US-Iran war that began in February this year, Iranian strikes hit US and Kuwaiti targets on Kuwaiti soil, including one that killed six US soldiers near Port Shuaiba.

Salman Al-Jawana, head of the political press section at the Kuwait Journalists Syndicate, told Al-Araby Al-Jadeed the agreement “should not be read as an ordinary bilateral pact, but in the context of reshaping the security environment in the Gulf after the escalation of regional threats”.

Pakistan’s own advantages help explain why it is a beneficiary of that reshaping.

Karim pointed out that Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed country in the Muslim world.

It also occupies a rare diplomatic space: It is a central mediator in the war between the US and Iran, its leadership trusted by both countries, while also managing strong relations with Arab nations in the Middle East and China, the rising superpower that the region’s nations want to woo.

That allows countries that have traditionally relied on a US security umbrella to expand their options without upsetting Washington in the way a similar set of deals with China might have.

What Islamabad gains is less settled than what it provides.

Pakistan received a record $41.6bn in remittances in the last financial year, according to the State Bank of Pakistan, with close to half coming from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Field Marshal Munir told Pakistani businessmen in 2023 that Gulf states could invest up to $100bn in the country. Three years on, delivered investment remains a fraction of that figure.

Karim said that what Pakistan could expect from Kuwait remains unclear.

“It is not clear what Pakistan will gain in return, but most likely the support from Kuwait can come in the form of subsidised energy supplies, though that will only mature if the Strait of Hormuz saga ends in one manner or another. Kuwait may also open up visas for Pakistani workers,” he said. The country is currently home to about 95,000 Pakistanis.

Mahmood framed the wider gain in starker terms.

“Any strategic cooperation of this kind makes you far more relevant, and that relevance now extends well beyond the region,” he told Al Jazeera.

The former military official said the Kuwait agreement could also potentially “strengthen our economic relationships” and help address some of Pakistan’s economic challenges.

“There are, of course, risks, particularly given the kind of conflict in the region, which becomes extremely dangerous if fought along sectarian lines. But they are far outweighed by the advantages Pakistan is gaining, and will continue to gain, from this strategic approach going forward,” he said.

articles.title: US-Israel war on Iran, six months down the line: In numbers
articles.summary: Al Jazeera tracks six months of the Iran war, from the dead and displaced to the shock delivered to the global economy.
articles.body:
Six months ago today , the United States and Israel launched their first strikes of on Iran, assassinating Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in Tehran and hitting nuclear and military sites around the country.

Those attacks prompted Iran to begin strikes on US military assets and infrastructure in Gulf countries – and for the Lebanese armed group, Hezbollah, to fire rockets into northern Israel, prompting near-daily Israeli responses since then and, at one point, control over one-fifth of Lebanon.

Neither side has gained the upper hand since. Iran has used its control of the Strait of Hormuz to squeeze Washington and global energy markets, and the conflict has settled into a stalemate, which months of negotiation have not broken.

Al Jazeera tracks the first six months of the war, from the numbers killed and displaced to the shock suffered by the global economy.

According to the latest official figures, at least 4,350 people are confirmed killed in Lebanon, 3,527 in Iran and 28 in Gulf states since the war began on February 28.

A further 60 Israelis and 18 US service members have been killed in Iranian attacks. The Pentagon says 757 US personnel have been wounded.

Figures are compiled from national health ministries and official bodies, and may change as the situation evolves and more information becomes available.

According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (ACLED), a US-based conflict monitoring group, the US and Israel have carried out at least 3,580 attacks on Iran since February 28. Over the same period, Iran carried out at least 2,053 attacks across the Gulf and the wider Middle East.

Before the war, at least 100 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day, more than half of them tankers, carrying tens of millions of barrels of oil, as well as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and other petrochemicals.

That collapsed within days of the war beginning. After the IRGC announced the strait’s closure on March 2, traffic fell to an average of five vessels a day and stayed there through the April ceasefire and the US blockade of Iranian ports.

The June 17 interim agreement increased the daily average to 20, but still only one-fifth of normal traffic, before the US resumed its blockade on July 14 and traffic sank back to five per day.

In the six months since fighting began, an average of seven vessels a day have passed through the strait.

Attacks on dozens of vessels have also been responsible for the decrease in shipping.

According to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), there have been 70 confirmed incidents involving ships in the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in 19 seafarer fatalities as of August 26.

War has cost the US $37.5bn … and counting

Last month, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a Senate hearing that the war had cost $37.5bn so far, up from about $25bn in late April and roughly $30bn in July. He said the total included payroll, operations, maintenance and anticipated costs through to the end of the budget year on September 30.

The true figure is likely higher. US media have reported the Pentagon’s internal estimate at $80bn to $100bn, including repairs to damaged US bases, replacing destroyed aircraft and replenishing weapons stocks.

The administration has not published an itemised breakdown.

Oil price is 22 percent higher than pre-war

Since the start of the war, Brent crude has risen roughly 22 percent, from $72.48 a barrel to $88.58 on August 28. It peaked at $120.88 on April 30, 67 percent higher than its pre-war level, after six months of volatile trading.

US oil reserve at lowest level since 1982

The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the government’s emergency stockpile of crude oil, has fallen to 290 million barrels, about 41 percent of its 714-million-barrel capacity and its lowest level since November 1982.

Other countries have released stocks too. The US pledge was the largest national share of a coordinated release of 400 million barrels agreed on March 11 by the 32 member countries of the International Energy Agency – the largest emergency stock release in its history.

Despite a ceasefire agreement between Lebanon and Israel that took effect on April 17 and was renewed on June 26, Israeli forces continue to occupy parts of Lebanon and carry out attacks.

Before the ceasefire, Israeli forces occupied nearly one-fifth of Lebanon – about 2,000sq km (770sq miles). A buffer zone covering roughly six percent of the country remains in place.

Fighting resumed on March 2, after Iran-backed Hezbollah fired at Israel in support of Tehran, three days into the US-Israeli war on Iran. Israel responded with a major offensive in Lebanon, killing at least 4,350 people over the months since and leaving 12,510 injured, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health.

Trump’s approval rating has fallen to the lowest of his presidency.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll, which closed on August 24, found that 33 percent of Americans approved of his performance in the White House and 65 percent disapproved, matching the December 2017 low of his first term.

The poll found that 80 percent of Americans, including 87 percent of Democrats and 71 percent of Republicans, think US involvement in Iran “will go on for an extended period of time”. Just 16 percent expect it to end within weeks.
