articles.title: Ugandan King Oyo Nyimba, once world’s youngest monarch, dies at 34
articles.summary: KAMPALA — Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king who became the world’s youngest ​reigning monarch when he took the crown in 1995, has died aged 34, the prime minister of his kingdom announced.
articles.body: KAMPALA — Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king who became the world’s youngest ​reigning monarch when he took the crown in 1995, has died aged 34, the prime minister of his kingdom announced. Uganda is a republic, ruled by an elected head of state, but it has several ⁠traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms as they were constituted in the pre-colonial period. Their political power is largely symbolic, but they wield enormous cultural and social influence. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV was the King of Tooro, a small kingdom ⁠in Uganda’s west near the border with ​the Democratic ⁠Republic of Congo. “It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty the Omukama ⁠of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV,” the prime minister of ​the kingdom, ⁠Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said ‌in a post on X late on Thursday. The king died at around 10:00 p.m. local time on Thursday, Akiiki said, without revealing the cause of ‌his death. Rukidi IV was crowned at just three ‌years old on September 12, 1995 after the death of his father, Rukirabasaija Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III. Balaam Barugahara, a minister in the government of President Yoweri Museveni, said shortly before ⁠the announcement of the king’s death that he was receiving treatment in the U.S. “This is an immeasurable loss,” the prime minister said, adding that the king, who was unmarried, had left an heir and that “continuity of the Crown is assured.” His death triggered an outpouring of grief across social media platforms in Uganda and widespread media coverage nationally. “Most devastating news! May His Majesty the ‌King’s soul rest in eternal peace,” Bobi Wine, Ugandan pop star-turned-politician who ​is the country’s leading opposition leader, said in a post on ‌X. In April, in a message to ⁠celebrate the King’s birthday, Tooro’s prime minister had said: “Our King is ⁠not distant from the realities of his people; he is part of this generation, part of this ‌ecosystem, growing, learning, and ​leading... His youth is not a limitation; ‌it is a strength. It brings ​energy, fresh perspective, and the courage to imagine a different future for Tooro.”

articles.title: Armed raid on cattle camp kills at least 49 in South Sudan
articles.summary: Thirty-three people were also wounded as gunmen raided village and seasonal cattle camp in northwest of the country.
articles.body:
An armed raid on a seasonal cattle camp and village in the northwest of South Sudan has killed least 49 people, according to local officials.

The raid, which also wounded 33 people, took place early on Thursday, as gunmen attacked the Machar-Pakuek cattle camp and Mading Juer Boma in Majak Payam, Tonj North County, Warrap State, according to an official statement.

The young African nation is plagued by violent cattle raids, with herders competing for scarce grazing lands and water for their livestock.

“The attack was perpetuated by an armed cross-border, criminal network,” said Warrap spokesperson William Wol Mayom Bol.

“We extend heartfelt condolences to the families that lost loved ones in the attack and appeal for restraint,” he added.

The local government condemned the attack and called on humanitarian organisations to help respond to the “humanitarian catastrophe resulting from conflict-induced displacement”.

The attack comes barely three weeks after another raid in the same area left 60 people dead and 50 wounded.

Last year, President Salva Kiir declared a six-month state of emergency across South Sudan amid a surge of violent inter-communal cattle raids.

Earlier this month, the head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), Anita Kiki Gbeho, expressed concerns over the cycle of communal violence in places such as Warrap.

articles.title: 'What exactly needed fact-checking?' Amit Malviya jibes amid Sonia Gandhi memoir row
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: BJP leader Amit Malviya on Friday took a dig at Congress leader Sonia Gandhi over Penguin Random House India’s decision to \"fact-check her .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP leader Amit Malviya on Friday took a dig at Congress leader Sonia Gandhi over Penguin Random House India’s decision to "fact-check her memoir", questioning whether the exercise was meant to verify the author’s memories or address what he described as “the blurred line between fact and fiction”.Malviya said it was “rather amusing” that the publisher felt the need to fact-check a memoir written by Sonia Gandhi herself."It is rather amusing that Penguin Random House India felt the need to fact-check Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, a book authored by Sonia Gandhi herself. The publisher says fact-checking is a normal part of the publishing process and that it remained “willing and keen” to publish the book. Fair enough," Malviya said in a post on X."But if a publisher has to fact-check a memoir written by its own author, perhaps the obvious question is: what exactly needed fact-checking - the author’s memories, or the blurred line between fact and fiction?" he added.The remarks came after Penguin Random House India clarified on Friday that it is not the publisher of Congress leader Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love in India. The publishing house also rejected reports that it had decided against publishing the book because Sonia Gandhi declined to accept editorial changes.In a statement posted on X, the publishing house said it had remained “willing and keen to publish” the memoir and stressed that fact-checking and providing editorial recommendations are a routine part of the publishing process.The clarification comes weeks after US publisher Alfred A Knopf, an imprint of Penguin Random House, announced that Belonging would be released on November 10. However, the memoir’s publisher or distributor in India remains unclear.An e-commerce listing has shown an e-book edition of Belonging available for pre-order at Rs 2,615, with William Collins, an imprint of HarperCollins UK, listed as the publisher.According to Alfred A Knopf, the memoir by 79-year-old Sonia Gandhi will offer a personal account of her life, spanning her childhood in post-war Italy, her marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family and the assassination of her husband, former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi.The book will also chronicle her entry into the “public world of politics” following Rajiv Gandhi’s assassination and her decision to decline the post of prime minister in 2004.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.Here are more Raksha Bandhan wishes, Bhadra kaal and Shubh Muhurat from The Times of India.

articles.title: Tropical Storms Karina and Lowell form in the Pacific Ocean as Dolly churns in the Atlantic
articles.summary: Tropical Storms Karina and Lowell formed Thursday in the Pacific Ocean, both of which were expected to become hurricanes in the next few days, the National Hurricane Center said.
articles.body: MIAMI — Tropical Storms Karina and Lowell formed Thursday in the Pacific Ocean, both of which were expected to become hurricanes in the next few days, the National Hurricane Center said. Tropical Storm Karina was located about 825 miles (1,330 kilometers) south of the southern tip of Baja California, with maximum sustained winds of around 45 mph (75 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center. Tropical Storm Lowell was about 1,765 miles (2,840 kilometers) west-southwest of the tip of Baja California, with maximum sustained winds of around 40 mph (65 kph). There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect for either storm, though the hurricane center warned swells from Karina could bring life-threatening surf and rip currents to portions of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula over the weekend. Earlier Thursday, Tropical Storm Dolly formed in the Atlantic Ocean far from land, and forecasters said it could bring heavy rain to portions of the Caribbean. The storm was about 1,555 miles (2,500 kilometers) east of the Leeward Islands and had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (64 kph), the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said. Dolly was moving west. The storm and its name had no connection to Dolly Parton’s death Tuesday. Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organization, and the lists of names are reused every six years. For the Atlantic region, the lists are alphabetical and alternate male and female names. Dolly was the fourth named storm for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season. There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but the center said the Leeward Islands could get heavy rain Saturday and Sunday. The Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola could see heavy rain Sunday and Monday. Little change in strength is forecast during the coming days, the center said, but flash flooding could occur. The Atlantic hurricane season started with Tropical Storm Arthur coming ashore on the U.S. Gulf Coast in June, and Tropical Storm Bertha dumped rain in Louisiana and Texas in July. Tropical Storm Cristobal formed and quickly dissipated in the Atlantic earlier in August. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast a below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to El Nino. It forecast eight to 14 named storms, with three to six of them reaching hurricane strength and one to three of those intensifying to major hurricanes. The NHC and other weather agencies name storms to easily communicate warnings about them to people and to avoid confusion. The WMO says names are chosen to be short, easy to pronounce and familiar to the regions of the world where the storm names are used. It meets regularly to evaluate potential names, and some names are retired for reasons of sensitivity, particularly for deadly or destructive storms. One name from the 2025 season was retired, Melissa, which was a Category 5 hurricane that brought devastation to the Caribbean.

articles.title: Dog missing for 12 years reunited with Chicago family
articles.summary: It’s a story straight out of Hollywood for a suburban Evanston woman, as she was reunited with a dog missing for a staggering 12 years.
articles.body: It’s a story straight out of Hollywood for a suburban Evanston woman, as she was reunited with a dog missing for a staggering 12 years. Vanessa Antonino lost her beloved dog Flor 12 years ago on the north side of Chicago, but this week, an incredible reunion took place as a volunteer organization was able to bring a long-running mystery to an end. Antonino told NBC Chicago she went to work like normal on that fateful day 12 years ago, and when she returned, Flor was gone. “There was a time in my life when I wasn’t put together. I was from place to place, living in my car, staying in my car, and Flor was there with me through everything,” she said. “And one day, I just went to work. I left her in the car like always, and when I came back out, she was gone.” At the time, Flor was 4 years old, and Antonino said she’s thought about the dog every day since. “I had not fully given up on her, but it’s just like ‘so many years had passed,’ and I was like ‘I don’t think I’ll ever see her again,’” she said. In those intervening 12 years, Antonino had four children, and she would frequently show the kids Flor’s picture, describing her as their big sister. Then, in a staggering stroke of fortune, there was a break in the mystery. According to officials at the Evanston Animal Shelter, Flor was found recently in Gary, Indiana, after devastating severe weather tore through the region. “There was a lady from Louisiana who was helping with the storm damage in Indiana, and she actually found Flor near some roads, and so she was obviously scared she was going to get hit,” volunteer Gillian Primavera said. After she was rescued, Flor ended up at Griffith Animal Control, and that’s when Microchip Hunters came into the picture. The organization researches what are known as “dead-end” microchips, which are difficult to trace back to their source or have outdated contact information from the owner, according to Jeanette Garlow, the co-Director of Lost Dogs Illinois. Garlow said in Flor’s case, the phone number associated with her microchip was not current. A volunteer from the Evanston Animal Shelter transported the pup from Illinois to Evanston, and the happy reunion was like a dream for Antonino. “I went and saw her. I just bawled,” she said. “I broke down completely. She was back with me. A piece of my heart was back with me.” Garlow said the story is a worthwhile reminder to microchip all pets, and to keep contact information current, because a reunion can still be possible, even a decade later. “Accidents happen, and once a pet is missing, it is too late to have them microchipped,” Garlow said.

articles.title: Scott Brown on Ruthless: Sophie Cunningham has the guts to challenge men competing in women’s sports
articles.summary: Former Sen. Scott Brown, who is running for the U.S. Senate again in New Hampshire, sat down with the "Ruthless" podcast and discussed his support WNBA star Sophie Cunningham.
articles.body: In an interview with the Ruthless Podcast, Scott Brown, former U.S. Senator and current Senate candidate in New Hampshire, commended Indiana Fever shooting guard Sophie Cunningham for her advocacy on behalf of women’s sports. "I don’t miss a game when the [Indiana] Fever [are] playing," Brown said in an interview released Friday morning. "Sophie Cunningham had the guts to get up and challenge this crazy ideology and put up with that crap." Cunningham made news earlier this summer when she said that female athletes shouldn’t have to compete against biological men. SEN RON JOHNSON DETAILS SENATE FILIBUSTER STRATEGY ON ‘RUTHLESS' Brown is no newcomer to the women’s sports debate. His daughter, Ayla, was a basketball player at Boston College. "My daughter committed to Boston College at 15," Brown, who served as ambassador to New Zealand during President Donald Trump's first term, said. "[She was a] Gatorade Player of the Year, two years in a row, 2,358 points in high school. And they had men, practice players, coming in and trying to make them better because they were bigger and stronger. To think one of them was going to take my baby's job." Earlier this month, Brown criticized the Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA) in an opinion piece in the Union Leader over its policies regarding transgender athletes. "It's hypocritical," Brown said of the league to the Fellas in the interview. "It's a no-brainer. The WNBA better get their you-know-what together because they're going to lose it all without even blinking." NEW HAMPSHIRE CANDIDATE JOHN SUNUNU BLASTS DEMS FOR MOVING ‘FIRST IN THE NATION PRIMARY’ ON RUTHLESS Brown is currently running for Senate, looking to replace the retiring Jeanne Shaheen. Brown shocked the political world with his January 2010 Massachusetts U.S. Senate in Massachusetts, defeating Martha Coakley in a special election to finish the term of the late Sen. Ted Kennedy. In the Republican primary on Sept. 8, Brown faces another former senator: John Sununu. Ruthless interviewed Sununu earlier this month. On the Democratic side, Rep. Chris Pappas faces several challengers, including Karishma Manzur." The general election will take place on November 3rd. CLICK HERE TO FOLLOW THE RUTHLESS PODCAST The interview took place as part of the Ruthless Midterm Interview Series, an ongoing initiative to interview major candidates across the country. The hosts have already interviewed candidates in 19 states, with more scheduled ahead of the November midterms. Podcast co-host Josh Holmes commended Brown for his commitment to conservative values in a region not known to be easy for Republicans. "You're a good man," Holmes told Brown. "I'm glad you stayed in it for as long as you have because you've been a real warrior in a bunch of places that aren't easy to be for sure."

articles.title: STEPHEN MOORE: Data centers aren’t just buildings. They are economic engines
articles.summary: Google has invested over $20 billion in Council Bluffs, Iowa, transforming the transcontinental railroad's Mile Zero into a data center crossroads.
articles.body: On November 17, 1863, Abraham Lincoln signed an executive order fixing the eastern terminus of the transcontinental railroad at Council Bluffs, Iowa. A modest town on the Missouri River became Mile Zero of the infrastructure that built industrial America. By the early 20th century, eight major railroads ran through Council Bluffs, and a farm-state river crossing had become one of the great junction points of the American economy. A century and a half later, Council Bluffs is Mile Zero again. In 2007, Google chose this town of 62,000 for one of its first company-built data centers. The company recognized, as Lincoln did, that America's infrastructure runs through the middle of the country. What’s also clear today are the extraordinary benefits that flow to the states and cities hosting 21st century infrastructure, such as data centers. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES Consider Iowa, where Google has now invested more than $20 billion since breaking ground in Council Bluffs. The investment is ongoing. Last year, the company committed another $7 billion to expand its presence in Council Bluffs and build an entirely new campus in Cedar Rapids. Google is not alone in committing capital to Iowa. Meta operates one of its largest data center campuses in Altoona. Microsoft has poured billions into West Des Moines. The state that critics once flew over has become the crossroads of the cloud. SILICON VALLEY IS LOSING THE DATA CENTER FIGHT, RISKING A REPEAT OF A CLASSIC FAILURE A small but vocal band of pressure groups claim that data centers are big buildings with few workers inside. But judging a data center by the headcount is like judging the transcontinental railroad by the number of stationmasters. The wealth was never in the depot. It was in everything the depot made possible. Look at what the buildout actually creates. Google is funding a partnership with an entity known as the electrical training ALLIANCE. It was created by the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers and the National Electrical Contractors Association and the partnership will massively expand Iowa's electrical workforce pipeline. Seven hundred apprentices will be trained in Cedar Rapids by 2030. META OFFERS PAID TRAINING FOR AI DATA CENTER JOBS These are careers in the skilled trades: electricians, pipefitters, welders, HVAC technicians. No four-year degree, no student debt. A high school graduate in eastern Iowa can walk into an apprenticeship and wire the machines that run the artificial intelligence economy. Construction of a single campus puts more than a thousand tradesmen to work for years at a time. And the ripple effects reach Main Street: Google's presence generated $2.7 billion in economic activity for Iowa last year. That translates to high-paying jobs for Iowa workers throughout the state. The community dividends are just as concrete. When Google learned that some Council Bluffs students had laptops but no internet at home, it extended its own wireless network to serve them for free. The company has put millions into local schools and nonprofits and funded the city's free public Wi-Fi. It also committed to replenishing 120 percent of the water it consumes, starting with a $1.3 million Missouri River Basin conservation project. AMERICA'S AI BOOM IS A JOBS OPPORTUNITY, NOT AN EXCUSE FOR UNIVERSAL BASIC INCOME None of this happened by accident. Iowa's leaders — Governor Kim Reynolds, Senator Joni Ernst, local officials in both parties — competed for this investment with low taxes, sensible permitting, and a simple message: build here. Other states chose differently. They held hearings, added conditions, studied the question until the cranes went elsewhere. The capital didn't wait. It never does. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION This is the choice now facing hundreds of American communities, because the AI buildout is the largest infrastructure project in our history — bigger in real dollars than the railroads, rural electrification, or the interstate highways. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lincoln understood, even amid a brutal civil war, that laying the groundwork to bind the country together with iron and steam merited his firm commitment. That same resolve is needed today. The states and cities that welcome the technology companies laying the foundation for America’s economic future will, like Council Bluffs, reap the benefits of being at the junction points of the next American century.

articles.title: Serbia says convicted war criminal Mladić to be buried with ‘highest honors’
articles.summary: Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian-Serb general convicted of genocide, will be buried with the “highest military and state honors,” Serbia’s Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić announced Friday, according to the country’s state-run broadcaster.
articles.body: Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian-Serb general convicted of genocide, will be buried with the “highest military and state honors,” Serbia’s Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić announced Friday, according to the country’s state-run broadcaster. Mladić, 84, died at the UN Detention Unit in The Hague on Thursday, after serving 15 years of his life sentence. It was not clear whether the plans include a full state funeral for the convicted war criminal. The Serbian government did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. According to Vujić, the burial location would be decided by the Mladić family. Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić told the media that if “the family wishes for him to be buried in Serbia, we will organize everything in a decent and dignified manner.” Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” Mladić personally orchestrated some of the worst war crimes of the Balkan wars, including the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica massacre. More than 10,000 people, including many children, died during the two-year siege of Sarajevo and more than 7,000 Muslims, mostly men and boys were slaughtered within a few days in Srebrenica in July 1995. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) found him guilty of genocide, crimes against humanity, persecution, extermination, murder, terror, unlawful attacks on civilians and hostage-taking. Emir Suljagic, a Srebrenica survivor who heads the Srebrenica Memorial Center, said in a statement on Thursday that Mladić’s death “does not change much.” “It doesn’t bring back the dead. It doesn’t clear mass graves. It does not change judgment,” he said. “Now the hardest part of the job remains: not to let the truth, responsibility and memory die with him.” But despite being widely recognized as a war criminal, Mladić remains a popular figure among some Serbs. The plans to honor Mladić sparked a wave of criticism from the pro-European opposition in the country, but were welcomed by many nationalists. Some pro-government media in Serbia also referred to Mladić as a hero and questioned his treatment in The Hague. The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement expressing Moscow’s condolences to Mladić’s family and friends. Serbia has been one of Russia’s closest allies in Europe, despite Belgrade’s stated ambition to join the European Union. In the statement, the ministry also criticized the ICTY and said: “The Russian side consistently pointed out that the trial of R. Mladić in The Hague and the conditions of his detention were accompanied by disregard for his basic rights.” Mladić was also widely mourned in Republika Srpska, the ethnic Serb-controlled part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The entity’s Prime Minister Savo Minić praised Mladić as a national hero and memorial events were held in multiple locations across the region. Meanwhile, representatives of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Bosniak and Croat part of the country, criticized what they called attempts to “publicly glorify a convicted war criminal.” As Mladić’s health deteriorated in recent months, the right-wing Serbian government repeatedly campaigned for him to be released to a hospital in Belgrade. The most recent of these appeals was made by Vujić on Monday. Vujić said on Friday that he would send a letter to The Hague asking for an investigation into Mladić’s death and treatment. The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, the body that carries out the functions of the now-dissolved ICTY, said it would launch a full inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Mladić’s death, which is common practice when a high-profile prisoner dies.

articles.title: Trump admin restricts foreign student internships, warns universities could lose certification over CPT violations
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration warns US universities of potential loss of certifications for failing to comply with Curricular Practical Training (CPT) rules for foreign students, prompting some institutions to pause internship approvals.
articles.body: The Trump administration has warned US universities that they could lose certification to enrol international students if they fail to comply with federal rules governing Curricular Practical Training (CPT) work authorisations.A memo issued on August 24 by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said the agency had identified an increase in CPT authorisations that appeared to violate federal requirements, according to Reuters.CPT allows eligible international students to undertake internships or other practical training when the work is an integral part of their academic curriculum.The memo said the training must be connected to an established course of study.“Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enrol foreign students,” it said.The guidance has prompted some universities to suspend or review certain internship applications for international students.The University of California, Los Angeles said it had paused some CPT authorisations while examining the federal directive.“UCLA has paused certain Curricular Practical Training authorizations while it reviews recent federal guidance and determines next steps,” a university spokesperson said.The University of California, Berkeley said the August 24 memo was narrower and more direct than an earlier directive issued in mid-August, but included stricter requirements.Its international office said it was unlikely to process some internship work authorisation applications “in the near future” and advised affected students to plan accordingly.The university said it would continue processing CPT applications linked to degree requirements. It also said it would resume processing CPT applications for doctoral dissertation and master’s thesis research and consult legal experts on procedures to meet the new requirements.The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said the underlying regulations had not changed.“Nothing about these regulations has changed,” the department said. “However, schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated.”The warning is part of a broader campaign by the Trump administration targeting US universities. Federal agencies have opened investigations and threatened funding over issues including pro-Palestinian protests, diversity programmes, climate initiatives and transgender policies.The administration has also revoked visas held by some foreign students involved in pro-Palestinian protests. Officials have described some demonstrations as antisemitic or supportive of extremist groups.Protesters, including Jewish organisations, have rejected that description. They say criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and its occupation of Palestinian territories is not antisemitic and that support for Palestinian rights does not amount to support for extremism.The Justice Department has separately expanded its scrutiny of university admissions. On Thursday, it alleged that admissions practices at George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences favoured Black and Hispanic applicants.The university disputed the findings.“We are disappointed by the DOJ’s conclusions, which we believe are incorrect,” it said, adding that its admissions policies complied with the law and were not discriminatory.The Justice Department has made similar allegations against other universities and said it was seeking settlement talks. articles.title: Oneness or Hindu supremacy? RSS chief Bhagwat’s secretive New York hosts
articles.summary: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat is scheduled to speak at an event in New York on Saturday.
articles.body:
A visit by India’s Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat to the United States this week is being opposed by many activists, politicians and human rights groups in New York.

Bhagwat is scheduled to speak on Saturday at an event called the “Universal Oneness Celebration” at Madison Square Garden in New York, and is expected to draw more than 5,000 attendees, including multifaith leaders.

But while the event is being billed as an event for unity, the RSS – a Hindu majoritarian front that is the parent of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party – has repeatedly faced accusations back in India of contributing to the persecution of religious minorities, including Muslims and Christians.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani told local media on Tuesday that he does not support the upcoming event and called the RSS’s ideology “exclusionary.” Many human rights groups in the US, such as Hindus for Human Rights, have said in a statement that “Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus.”

The principal organiser of Saturday’s event is a US-based non-profit group called American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) Forum, which argues on its website that it seeks to promote intercultural understanding. But the website itself offers no details of those behind the group.

A deeper look at the group’s founding and registration documents, however, sheds light on its leaders – and their deep links to the RSS, which has long advocated for a Hindu-first vision for India, a country that has otherwise, through its millennia-long history, been home to people from many faiths.

So what is AHEAD Forum and who are the organisers of Bhagwat’s New York event?

The event, organised by AHEAD Forum, will take place from on Saturday 2:00pm to 15:30pm local time (19:00-21:30 GMT) in Madison Square Garden in New York.

According to AHEAD’s social media platforms, the event called “Universal Oneness Celebration” seeks to celebrate “diversity, dialogue, and the timeless Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.”

Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam is a Sanskrit phrase which translates to “the world is one family.”

India’s RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat has been invited as the event’s keynote speaker and comes more than a year after the RSS celebrated 100 years since its founding in 1925. Leaders from other faiths are also expected to attend.

But Apoorvanand, a Hindi professor at the University of Delhi who writes literary and cultural criticism, told Al Jazeera that the “unity” advertisements for the event refer to “Hindu unity”.

“The objective is to establish Hindu unity, which the RSS works for. It’s also about Hindu unity against Muslims and Christians,” he said.

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu volunteer organisation founded in 1925 by physician and Hindu nationalist Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in Nagpur, modern-day Maharashtra.

The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, sometimes called the Sangh for short, is Hindi for National Volunteer Organisation.

The RSS works across society, operating schools, hospitals, magazines and publishing houses, to advocate for the idea of Hindutva , a Hindu supremacist idea that aims to turn India from a constitutionally secular state into a Hindu one.

It describes itself as a “Hindu-centric civilisational, cultural movement” that aims to “carry the nation to the pinnacle of glory” and is often described as the ideological mothership of India’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

But the RSS has also been banned in India several times, including in 1948 after a former member assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

Currently, the RSS leads a network of more than 2,500 right-wing Hindu organisations called the Sangh Parivar, Hindi for “RSS family”.

Bhagwat, who was born in Chandrapur in the Indian state of Maharashtra, grew up in a family that supported RSS values and officially became the organisation’s member in 1975. He was appointed as the organisation’s chief in March 2009.

What is the controversy over the New York event?

Indian human rights groups, activists and also New York’s Mayor Mamdani have opposed the event.

When asked by local media on Tuesday about stopping the event, Mamdani said that as the first Indian-American mayor of New York, it has “been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision”.

He acknowledged that he grew up in India, which he said was “a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India.”

He, however, added that he was not sure if, as mayor of New York, he could stop a private organisation’s event.

In a statement published on August 19, Sravya Tadepalli, deputy executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, said, “Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He represents the fringe, extremist Hindu nationalist movement, which has engaged in hate and violence against religious minority communities for a century.”

“In 1939, Madison Square Garden hosted a Nazi rally, which any of us can look back on and feel shock and shame. Madison Square Garden should not make the same mistake by holding a rally celebrating the leader of a hate movement like Hindu nationalism,” Tadepalli added.

Amid these remarks, the RSS has defended Bhagwat’s goals at the upcoming event.

On Thursday, senior RSS functionary Sunil Ambekar said, “The Universal Oneness Celebration in New York exemplifies an interfaith gathering.”

He said that Bhagwat would “communicate with a diverse, multicultural and multi-faith audience”.

AHEAD Forum describes itself as an organisation that “builds bridges between communities worldwide through understanding and mutual respect”.

According to its website, the group has chapters across major US cities including New York, Boston, Atlanta, Dallas, Chicago, Washington, DC an Houston, among others.

AHEAD Forum was registered as a nonprofit organisation in May 2025. According to the Internal Revenue Service (the US tax agency), the Forum filed for tax exemption in September 2025.

At the end of 2025, the tax filing shows that AHEAD had generated revenue of $61,409 – all of it from contributions. AHEAD also had assets worth $61,124 in the last fiscal year.

While US IRS data shows that AHEAD’s current directors are Sudesh Agrawal, Naresh Rajanna and Rasita Vishnuram, a report published by Savera, a coalition of US-based groups trying to combat the rise of Hindu nationalism, suggests direct links between the nonprofit and the RSS.

Al Jazeera has also independently verified a series of documents filed by AHEAD with US agencies that show these links.

The group listed an individual named Harish Kandpal as its bookkeeper in its filing with the IRS under its tax-exempt status in 2025.

But California’s listing of registered nonprofits and businesses shows that AHEAD Forum was, until earlier this year, listing Khanderao Kand, a long-time US-based leader of the RSS and its overseas wing, the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh (HSS), as its bookkeeper. The organisation, in fact, was originally registered to Kand’s address. The California database shows the registration was changed to Kandpal’s address in March 2026.

That, Savera said in its report , happened after Kand’s RSS links and his efforts to lobby in the US on behalf of the Hindu supremacist group were “exposed by investigative reporting”.

However, Kandpal and Kand have previously been colleagues at the Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies, another US-based group founded by Kand.

Meanwhile, Savera found that other leaders of the AHEAD Forum also have links to the RSS or to organisations close to the Modi government. Sudesh Agarwal, one of the directors of the nonprofit, heads the Cleveland chapter of the HSS, for instance.

Al Jazeera has reached out to AHEAD Forum for its response to the findings in Savera’s report, and accusations that it is attempting to mask the Hindu majoritarian leanings of its leaders, but is yet to receive a response.

Since 2015, several Muslims in India have been lynched by mobs during disputes about herding cattle or over allegations of eating beef. They have also fallen victim to targeted attacks.

Besides hate crimes against Indian Muslims, there has been a marked spike in hate crimes against Christians in India recently. According to a report published at the start of the year by India Hate Lab , a group that tracks hate crimes and speech in India, hate speech events targeting Christians rose from 115 in 2024 to 162 in 2025, a 41 percent increase.

Many instances of hate speech against Muslims and Christians have involved leaders of the BJP or other organisations in the broad RSS ecosystem.

However, in recent months, the RSS has been organising visits to the US and other Western countries to bolster its public image globally and dispel claims it is involved in violence against religious minority groups in India.

Saturday’s event is one such effort by the RSS and the event’s hosts, according to experts.

“The RSS is spreading its tentacles to collaborate with other right-wing organisations,” Apoorvanand said.

“They have expressed this intent very clearly in recent times that they want to establish a right reactionary network and be part of it. So they are looking for allies at events in the West with groups close to [US President Donald] Trump and his allies,” he said.

“I’m very sad that people who are enjoying American hospitality and freedom of speech and expression in the US, want to practice Hinduism in this way, where they use their resources to support an organisation which is responsible for marginalisation of Muslim, Christian and other minority communities within India.

“There could not be a more deceptive thing than this.”

articles.title: Fed has 'work to do' if price rises don't ease for Americans, Warsh says
articles.summary: Kevin Warsh remarks suggest interest rates could be increased if policymakers think inflation is running too high.
articles.body:
The head of the US central bank has said policymakers will "have work to do" if they were not confident cost-of-living pressures were easing for Americans.

Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said while inflation readings looked better than expected over the summer, they did not show that the current picture had "meaningfully improved".

The new Fed boss stressed that his remarks should not be treated as a guide for future interest rate decisions, but the comments are a signal rates could be raised if policymakers believe inflation is too high.

Latest figures show prices rose 3.4% in the year to July, above the Fed's 2% target. Another inflation measure closely watched by the Fed is running at 3.7%.

Warsh made the comments in his first speech at the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming, which sees central bankers, government officials and academics from around the world gather to talk about interest rates, inflation and other economic issues.

Warsh said given prices were rising by more than 2% on annual basis, "the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices".

"Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do."

The central bank boss has remained tight-lipped about the potential path of interest rates, but investors will have watched his speech closely for any signs of the Fed's approach under his leadership.

The central bank's next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September.

The reaction to any decision of US President Donald Trump will be closely watched, with the mid-term elections looming and voters concerned about affordability.

Trump, who appointed Warsh in May, repeatedly criticised and pushed his predecessor Jerome Powell to cut interest rates. The president has previously said rate hikes "just keeps the country down".

Warsh issued a plea in his speech to not label his remark as "forward guidance" and said he believed the practice of sending signals to the markets on future interest rate decisions, adopted in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, had "overstayed its welcome".

"Oversharing policy deliberations and overcommitting to future decisions can lead markets, businesses, and households astray," he said, adding it also inhibited the Fed the "freedom to make the right calls when it's time to decide".

Interest rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row amid concerns over inflation due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

Following Warsh's remarks, the rates market showed growing expectations of an interest rate rise in September, according to CME data.

Analysts at Capital Economics said Warsh's speech delivered a "far clearer - and hawkish - message" and that it left "the door open to a hike" earlier than previously expected.

"Hikes are not guaranteed, but Warsh is now at least suggesting he is on board with them if economic growth remains strong and monthly core PCE [Personal Consumption Expenditures] price growth remains a bit too firm," they said.

Why the US economy is ringing alarm bells

'No magic wand' to tackle high prices, Fed boss says as US interest rates held

Higher oil prices has also fuelled bond market investors, who have demanded higher returns, leading to higher borrowing costs for the US government and other major corporations.

Such borrowing costs impact the cost of borrowing for mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

The spike in interest payments has driven US national debt past the $40tn (£29.5tn). The figure has doubled in a decade under both the Trump and Joe Biden administrations.

The figure is rising by about $90,000 (£66,500) every second, or $7.8bn a day, according to the Congress Joint Economic Committee.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the government would buy back more debt in a bid to lower borrowing costs, but the market's reaction to the announcement proved short lived.

Interest rate hikes are a tool used by central banks aiming to slow the pace prices are rising in the shops. By pushing up the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, central bankers hope consumers will spend less and the rate of price increases will slow.

Higher interest rates, however, can lead to better returns for savers.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy is ‘scared’ as jury in her murder trial continues deliberations
articles.summary: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy is “scared” as the jury continues its second day of deliberations to determine whether she is guilty of killing her three children in 2023, her defense lawyer said Friday.
articles.body: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy is “scared” as the jury continues its second day of deliberations to determine whether she is guilty of killing her three children in 2023, her defense lawyer said Friday. “She’s nervous. Sad. Scared. Same as she has been,” Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington told reporters at the courthouse Friday, according to NBC Boston. There’s an anxiousness in the air and reporters were lining the hallways at Plymouth Superior Court as the murder trial is in its home stretch after five weeks of testimony from more than 80 witnesses. Deliberations resumed Friday at 9:15 a.m., and the jury had its first question around 10 a.m., about four hours into deliberations. Judge William Sullivan called a recess after the question was brought to his attention, just after he called the opposing attorneys into sidebar. The question was not publicly disclosed, and the jury was never brought into the courtroom. Clancy’s mother, father and sister sat in court Friday behind her. Reddington, however, told reporters in Plymouth that the jury wanted to see the bag of pills he showed during closings, as well as some other pill bottles and a knife that were all entered as evidence in the case. It’s typical for a jury to have questions as it deliberates, especially in such a winding case with competing storylines and troves of evidence. Juries are also known to ask questions about the instructions given by the judge, and the law and how to apply it. Clancy, 36, is facing charges of fatally strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023. The jury — comprised of nine women and three men — must decide if Clancy is guilty of first-degree murder in relation to the killings. If she is convicted of first-degree murder, she faces life in prison. Throughout the trial, the defense has argued that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she carried out the murders, before trying to kill herself by hurling herself out of her Duxbury, Massachusetts, home’s second-story window. Reddington has said that Clancy was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations, a symptom of the postpartum psychosis, while her then-husband was out running errands that night. The prosecution, though, argued that even though Clancy was clearly struggling with her mental health, she was not actually in psychosis and therefore had control over her actions. They have said that Clancy deliberately chose to kill her kids before trying to kill herself, and that she planned out their murders earlier that evening. The jury also has the option to convict her of lesser charges, including second-degree murder and manslaughter, or to deem her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility — meaning that they believe she did kill the children, but couldn’t control her actions due to being in psychosis. Both the prosecution and the defense offered their closing arguments Thursday morning, and the jury began deliberating that afternoon. Sullivan has said that if Clancy is found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, the district attorney or another authority will likely petition the court to commit her to a mental health facility. It is unclear what her sentencing will look like if she is convicted of a lesser charge.

articles.title: Board of Peace envoy Mladenov warns Gaza ceasefire risks ‘collapse’
articles.summary: In an interview with Al Jazeera, Nicolay Mladenov says that a return to war would be ‘devastating’.
articles.body:
The failure of both sides to adhere to the roadmap for peace “threatens a collapse of the ceasefire in Gaza”, Nikolay Mladenov, the high representative for the Board of Peace, has warned in an interview with Al Jazeera.

There is “no better alternative to the current plan”, Mladenov said on Friday, adding that the “return to war would be devastating”.

His warning was “directed at both the Palestinian and Israeli sides”, he said, at a time when the besieged Strip is witnessing continued Israeli raids and attacks.

Mladenov stressed that any retreat from the commitments of the roadmap will negatively affect overall security and humanitarian arrangements in Palestine, which may return the region to a spiral of violence with dire consequences.

The Board of Peace has “determined the mechanism for deploying the International Stabilization Force [ISF] and its deployment locations in the Gaza Strip,” he said, noting that Morocco agreed to take part, though Turkiye will not participate after Israel vetoed Ankara’s involvement.

He added that the force’s “advance elements should arrive in the Gaza Strip soon”.

On reconstruction, Mladenov told Al Jazeera that the Board has received pledges worth $7bn, while crediting Qatar, Egypt and Turkiye with playing “an important role” in advancing the agreement with Hamas.

He noted talks with Israel on increasing humanitarian aid are “good”, while expressing hope that a Palestinian national committee would “assume its responsibilities in the Gaza Strip soon”.

The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza is a proposed technocratic, non-factional authority tasked with running day-to-day civil affairs. It is designed to manage public services and coordinate local reconstruction independently of Hamas and other political factions.

Mladenov first proposed a 15-point roadmap on May 21, covering reconstruction, disarmament of Palestinian armed groups, an Israeli gradual withdrawal, and the ISF’s mandate, alongside restructuring Gaza’s police.

The Board of Peace announced on July 31 that it had reached an agreement on the roadmap for the ceasefire’s next phase. Hamas said it had approved it and called on Israel to be held to its implementation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently rejected the plan, denying reports that his government had agreed to allow the international troops into Gaza at all. This leaves the roadmap’s status publicly contested even as the US and the Board of Peace said it’s the only viable path forward.

On the ground, Israel’s violations of the ceasefire have continued unabated. Since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, 1,303 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire, and 4,336 more were wounded, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

The overall toll from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023 stands at 73,438 killed and 174,447 wounded, the ministry said.

Mladenov’s warning also comes amid renewed, if uncertain, diplomatic movement.

In recent weeks, Hamas’s political chief Khalil al-Hayya held talks with Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, before a visit to the region by US envoy Jared Kushner aimed at narrowing the gap between Israel and the Board of Peace’s plan.

The trip followed Netanyahu’s public rejection of the roadmap, with a US official saying Washington and Israel remain aligned on “the strategic goal” but that Israel has expressed “doubts” requiring further coordination.

Analysts say the roadmap’s political viability still hinges on securing genuine Israeli buy-in, which has remained unresolved despite Hamas’s stated approval and months of mediation efforts.

articles.title: Andy Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying unlike Starmer
articles.summary: Burnham has called for all views to be respected as MPs vote in two weeks on legalising assisted dying in England and Wales.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has revealed he will not vote on the assisted dying bill for England and Wales unlike his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

MPs are likely to get the chance to debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill in two weeks' time.

The bill is identical to the one put to Parliament last year, where it passed in the House of Commons but stalled in the Lords after an unprecedented number of amendments meant it ran out of time .

Burnham said he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide". Starmer voted in favour of the previous bill when he was PM but did not campaign in favour of it, remaining officially neutral.

Writing to Labour MPs on Friday, Burnham said: "My role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of Parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not.

"I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote.

"For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at Second Reading."

He added that "there is no single right position" and it was an "incredibly important and personal debate".

"It is vital that those different views are treated with dignity and respect," he wrote.

While his abstension is a departure from Starmer's support , Burnham stressed that the government as an entity would officially remain neutral on the bill.

When he was Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham indicated he was in favour of assisted dying in principle.

But in June he suggested it would be challenging to implement before social and palliative care were improved.

The assisted dying law would allow adults over the age of 18 who are expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Burnham has also told ministers they can vote as they wish but, in a separate letter on Friday, he told them they "should avoid being part of the public debate and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department's responsibilities".

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper previously voted in favour of assisted dying, but her predecessor Wes Streeting had openly voiced concerns about the implications for the NHS.

Supporters of the assisted dying bill - brought by Labour MP Lauren Edwards - are hoping it will to pass the Commons unamended.

This is because an amended bill in the Commons would remove powers under the Parliament Acts to override the Lords and make it law if they refuse to back it.

MPs in favour of the bill hope Lords would vote in favour, if presented the choice of some sceptical amendments versus an entirely unamended bill becoming law.

It comes after the Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments, mainly from opponents, during the previous bill earlier this year.

That prompted assisted dying campaigner Dame Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer, to accuse opponents of trying to sabotage rather than scrutinise it.

Opponents of assisted dying have vowed to continue scrutinising the bill.

A separate bill that would have legalised assisted dying in Scotland was rejected by the Scottish Parliament in March 2026 .

articles.title: Jason Arday plagiarism accuser Nathan Cofnas faced doubts over expertise, 'far-right agenda' at Ghent
articles.summary: UK News: Nathan Cofnas, known for his plagiarism allegations against Jason Arday, faces severe criticism from academics at Ghent University questioning his qualifications and alleged far-right ideologies. The university has suspended him pending investigation amid concerns about the academic hiring process.
articles.body: Nathan Cofnas, the academic who exposed Cambridge University Sociology professor Jason Arday’s plagiarism, faced objections from fellow academics at Ghent University over his appointment to a postdoctoral research role.Cofnas joined the Belgian university in March for a project examining “the future of liberalism”. Soon after his appointment, professors of philosophy and moral sciences department raised questions about his suitability for the role, including his academic expertise and the process through which he was selected, The Guardian reported.The department submitted a 19-page statement to the university’s rector and the dean of the relevant faculty on May 28, after its council approved the document as its official position on the appointment on May 27.The academics questioned whether Cofnas had been the strongest candidate among 14 applicants. They said his background showed “very limited expertise” in political philosophy, liberalism and demography, which they identified as central to the research project.They also said the job requirement for a “strong research interest in liberalism” was not reflected in his publication record or CV.The concerns went beyond Cofnas's academic qualifications. The department said his appointment could hurt the university because of views associated with racial pseudoscience and what it described as a “far-right agenda”.Academics also questioned his work on intelligence, saying Cofnas had not conducted research in the field himself even though he had publicly written about intelligence and racial differences.“Cofnas himself has never conducted intelligence research, nor is such research envisaged within the project for which he was hired,” the department said.It added that views expressed by Cofnas in blog posts were “not based on his own scientific research” and were “simply not based on sound research”.Opposition to the appointment had emerged earlier. An email sent to Ghent's university leaders and governors in March was signed by 48 department staff, 73 students and 367 academics from Ghent and other universities. The signatories expressed “astonishment and indignation” over Cofnas's appointment.The philosophy department's statement also alleged that there had been insufficient transparency in the hiring process. Academics said a “large majority” suspected the appointment was “an ideological choice … decided in advance”.Cofnas has previously attracted attention for his views on race and intelligence. In a 2023 post on X (formerly Twitter), he wrote: “There are obviously personality differences between Jews and non-Jews … On average, Jews are better than gentiles at capitalising on their [general intelligence].”He also wrote an April 2023 Substack post titled “How to take back academia”, in which he discussed ways to “remove” academics he called “wokesters” by showing that they did not satisfy what he described as “minimal criteria”.Cofnas has defended his academic credentials and rejected the criticism surrounding his appointment.“My academic qualifications are a matter of public record,” he said.He also accused critics of trying to silence him over his views, saying: “The silliest accusation is that I am ‘uninterested in the academic exchange of ideas’. The people who said this are trying to get me fired or even thrown in jail for expressing my ideas.”Ghent University has since suspended Cofnas pending a “preliminary investigation”. The university has not said whether the disciplinary action is connected to the concerns raised over his appointment.A university spokesperson said Ghent would not comment on “the specific details of the disciplinary case or the underlying arguments”.In announcing the suspension, rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert said the university remained committed to academic freedom and open debate, including when opinions are controversial.“We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited,” they said.They added that academic freedom carries responsibility and may be restricted to protect the rights of others. The university said it took recent public statements by a postdoctoral researcher “very seriously” and had acted within its powers and the applicable framework.The dispute over Cofnas's position at Ghent has unfolded alongside the controversy surrounding his allegations against Arday. The University of Cambridge sociology professor was found dead on August 14 after facing intense scrutiny over his professional and personal achievements.The plagiarism allegations made against Arday have not been formally proven. In response to them, Arday acknowledged “mistakes” but said he had faced unacceptable cruelty.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Autopsy shows National Guard fatally shot Memphis man in the back
articles.summary: The report conflicts with the authorities’ initial account, which said Tyrin Johnson had been shot in the chest.
articles.body:
A bullet fired by members of the Tennessee National Guard entered the back of 20-year-old Tyrin Johnson, pierced his lung and killed him, an autopsy report shows, contradicting the initial account given by officials.

Authorities previously said that Johnson was shot by two guard members in the chest on 5 July in Memphis, after he faced them with a gun.

A copy of the autopsy seen by the BBC said that a single bullet penetrated his back on the right side before exiting through his upper right chest.

Johnson's family is calling for accountability following the release of the autopsy report. The National Guard did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.

"Be transparent - you shot him in the back," Evaniel Johnson, the slain 20-year-old's grandfather, told the Associated Press.

"I just want to make sure somebody be responsible for what happened. Some accountability. They ain't never going to bring my grandson back.

"If he ain't caused you no threat, you know what I'm saying, you have no reason to be killing," Johnson, a former Nashville correctional officer, added.

The autopsy was conducted by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center Office of the Medical Examiner.

Its report included the "investigative narrative" of an agent with the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation who said Memphis police and National Guard troops were first called to scene after reports of nearby gunfire.

They encountered Johnson, the investigative narrative said, who then "grabbed at his waistband".

"Law enforcement officers saw the unknown male draw a firearm," according to the officer's account of events, included in the report. "Law enforcement officers then shot at the unknown male, striking him once in the chest."

Separate from the officer's account, the report also said Johnson was carrying a "handgun magazine with rounds".

In Tennessee, gun laws allow legal gun owners to openly carry weapons.

"The autopsy findings reinforce the serious concerns we have regarding Tyrin's shooting and the circumstances surrounding his encounter with the Memphis Safe Task Force," the Johnson family's lawyer Andre Wharton, who shared the autopsy report with the BBC, said in a statement.

"The fact that Tyrin was actually shot in the back, contrasted with officer and task force's accounts, only further underscores the devastating nature of this encounter."

Johnson's cause of death was listed as "homicide", the official term used when a death is caused by another person. The term does not always include intent, and no criminal charges have been filed to date.

Asked by the BBC about the conflicting findings, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation referred to its original July statement, saying the investigation remained "active and ongoing".

"Reports that Tyrin Johnson turned and pointed a gun at National Guardsmen were not distributed by the TBI," the agency said.

Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson released a statement on X on Friday saying "Johnson should be alive today" and called for an investigation.

"The National Guard is not welcome here," he continued. "Mr Johnson's murder is a horrifying example of the brutality and injustice the Memphis Unsafe Task Force has brought to our city."

The troops were in Memphis as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, created by US President Donald Trump amid a larger effort to deploy National Guard troops to US cities.

Trump has said the troops deployment - largely in Democrat-led cities, including Chicago, Los Angeles and Washington DC - was meant to combat crime.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills three Palestinians in West Bank’s Jenin
articles.summary: Israel’s prime minister and defence minister praise the attack as Hamas calls for Israeli ‘crimes’ to stop.
articles.body:
The Israeli army has killed three Palestinians in Jenin in a rare air strike in the occupied West Bank, amid growing tensions in the territory.

In a statement, the Israeli military said it “eliminated” three people on Friday, one a Palestinian it described as a Hamas operative as well as two of his accomplices.

Hamas condemned the strike but did not claim the person targeted – whom the Israeli military identified as Qais Bitawi – as a member. Palestinian Islamic Jihad said in a statement Bitawi was a senior operative of its armed wing.

A spokesperson for the Israeli military said the strike targeted a car carrying the men.

The Palestine Red Crescent ambulance service said Israeli ground troops ⁠raided the site of the drone strike, briefly detained medics and ⁠prevented them from transporting those wounded or killed to hospital.

The Red Crescent said its personnel were also detained after arriving at the scene.

The Palestinian Wafa news agency reported that the Israeli drone strike had targeted a house under construction in the western area of Jenin City, and that three Palestinians were killed instantly.

Photos from the AFP news agency showed Israeli soldiers removing a body from a house under construction on the outskirts of Jenin.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu celebrated the strike in a post on X, calling it a “successful thwarting” of the three targeted individuals.

After the attack, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz congratulated the military, police and Shin Bet for the strike and said the Jenin camp has been “evacuated of residents”. He added that the Israeli military is now “permanently stationed there, like other terrorist camps” in the West Bank.

Hamas condemned the strike in a statement mourning “the martyrs who fell in the occupation’s bombing of Jenin,” saying that Palestinians “will continue to cling to their land and rights”.

The group called on the international community “to take immediate action to stop these crimes and end impunity” and hold Israel “fully responsible for the repercussions”.

The occupied West Bank, home to the Palestinian Authority, has seen soaring violence by Israeli settlers and soldiers but has recently avoided Israeli military strikes that have devastated the Gaza Strip since the genocidal war began on October 7, 2023.

Military raids on Palestinian towns in the West Bank are common, but Israel last carried out a strike there in February 2025.

Friday’s strike in Jenin comes as separate Israeli strikes in Gaza killed at least five people , and as Nikolay Mladenov, the high representative for the United States-led Board of Peace, warned that the failure of both sides to adhere to the roadmap for peace “threatens a collapse of the ceasefire in Gaza”.
